sections.title: 1. Locks (PcoMutex): Passive Waiting, Ownership & Recursion
sections.description: How mutexes eliminate active waiting, ownership semantics, recursive vs. non-recursive locks, and common locking traps.

blocks.title: Verrouille / Déverrouille & PcoMutex Semantics
PcoMutex: Protecting a Shared Counter (Slide 12)

annotations.note: Shared static PcoMutex (unlocked by default, NonRecursive).
Acquires ownership before entering the critical section (counter = counter + 1).
Releases ownership in the same function immediately after the critical section.

blocks.title: Mutex Traps: Cross-Thread Unlock, Recursion & Split Lock/Unlock (Slides 7, 15–17)

annotations.note: Violates ownership: only the thread that locked m may unlock it.
Default PcoMutex is non-recursive: second lock() by the same thread deadlocks.
Recursive mode counts nested locks by the same owner thread.
Public method calling another locked public method deadlocks unless mutex is recursive.
Splitting lock() and unlock() across functions risks forgetting unlock() on early returns or alternate call paths.

blocks.title: Mutex Ownership & Cross-Thread Signaling
blocks.front: Can Thread A lock a `PcoMutex` and have Thread B unlock it to signal an event? Why or why not?
blocks.back: **No!** A mutex has a strict **owner**—only the thread that acquired the lock is permitted to call `unlock()`. Furthermore, unlocking an already-unlocked mutex has no memory/counter effect. For cross-thread signaling (`T1 -> T2`), you must use a `PcoSemaphore`.
blocks.hint: Think about Slide 5, Slide 7, and Slide 18.

blocks.title: Recursive vs. Non-Recursive PcoMutex
blocks.front: What happens if a thread calls `lock()` twice on a default `PcoMutex`, and how does `PcoMutex::RecursionMode::Recursive` change this?
blocks.back:
* **Default (`NonRecursive`):** Instant **self-deadlock** on the second `lock()`.
* **`Recursive`:** The mutex remembers the **owner thread** and increments a **lock counter**. The owner can re-lock without blocking, and the mutex only becomes free after `unlock()` is called the **exact same number of times**.
blocks.hint: Think about the internal counter + owner tracking.

blocks.question: Which statement about a default (non-recursive) `PcoMutex` is TRUE?
options: Calling `unlock()` three times on an unlocked mutex leaves it unlocked with no cumulative effect, and calling `lock()` twice consecutively in the same thread causes a deadlock.
Calling `unlock()` three times increments an internal counter to 3, allowing three threads to enter simultaneously.
Any thread can call `unlock()` to release a mutex locked by another thread.
A `PcoMutex` starts locked after construction and must be unlocked in `main()` before threads use it.
blocks.correct_answer: Calling `unlock()` three times on an unlocked mutex leaves it unlocked with no cumulative effect, and calling `lock()` twice consecutively in the same thread causes a deadlock.
blocks.explanation: A non-recursive `PcoMutex` starts unlocked, has strict single-thread ownership, has no memory of extra `unlock()` calls, and self-deadlocks if the owner calls `lock()` again before `unlock()`.
hints: Does a mutex maintain a counter of extra unlocks like a semaphore?
What is the initial state of `PcoMutex mutex;`?

blocks.title: Dijkstra's P/V Pseudocode vs. PcoSemaphore
Controlled Section Example: Max 2 of 4 Threads Inside (Slide 28)

annotations.note: Initialized to 2: up to 2 threads can be inside the controlled section simultaneously.
The 3rd and 4th threads block in FIFO order until one of the first 2 calls release().

blocks.title: Dijkstra's Negative Counter vs. PcoSemaphore
blocks.front: In Dijkstra's `P(s)`/`V(s)` pseudocode, what does a negative value `s = -3` mean, and why can't you initialize `PcoSemaphore(-1)`?
blocks.back:
In Dijkstra's pseudocode, `s = -3` means **3 threads are currently blocked** in the semaphore's waiting queue (`V` checks `if (s <= 0)` to wake one).

In `PcoSemaphore(unsigned int n = 0)`, `n` is `unsigned int` because a semaphore cannot *start* with negative resources. Passing `-1` underflows to `UINT_MAX`, making the semaphore wide open instead of blocking.
blocks.hint: Check `P(s)` (`s -= 1; if (s < 0) ...`) and the C++ constructor signature.

blocks.title: Strong vs. Weak Semaphores
blocks.front: What is the difference between a **strong** (*fort*) and a **weak** (*faible*) semaphore, and which one is `PcoSemaphore`?
blocks.back:
* **Strong semaphore:** The waiting queue is ordered (**FIFO**)—threads are woken in their exact arrival order.
* **Weak semaphore:** The waiting queue is **unordered**—any waiting thread may be woken.

**`PcoSemaphore` is a strong (FIFO) semaphore.**
blocks.hint: Think about arrival order and starvation.

blocks.question: What is the effect of declaring `PcoSemaphore sem(-1);` in C++?
options: No useful effect: `-1` underflows when converted to `unsigned int`, initializing the semaphore to a huge positive value.
It calls `sem.acquire()` automatically inside the constructor.
It blocks the creating thread immediately upon declaration.
It creates a mutex instead of a semaphore.
blocks.correct_answer: No useful effect: `-1` underflows when converted to `unsigned int`, initializing the semaphore to a huge positive value.
blocks.explanation: The constructor signature is `PcoSemaphore(unsigned int n = 0)`. Passing `-1` implicitly converts `-1` to `unsigned int` (two's complement underflow to `4294967295`), so `acquire()` will not block!
hints: Check the parameter type of `PcoSemaphore::PcoSemaphore(unsigned int n = 0)`.
What happens in C++ when `-1` is passed to an `unsigned int` parameter?

blocks.question: In the Controlled Section example (`NB_THREADS = 4`, `PcoSemaphore(2)`), suppose T0 and T1 enter first, then T2 arrives, then T3 arrives. When T0 calls `sem->release()`, which thread is woken next?
options: T2, because `PcoSemaphore` is a strong (FIFO) semaphore.
Either T2 or T3 arbitrarily, because semaphores have unordered queues.
T3, because `PcoSemaphore` uses LIFO ordering.
Neither T2 nor T3 until T1 also calls `release()`.
blocks.correct_answer: T2, because `PcoSemaphore` is a strong (FIFO) semaphore.
blocks.explanation: `PcoSemaphore` is a strong semaphore, meaning its waiting queue is strictly FIFO. Since T2 arrived before T3, T2 is woken first when T0 releases a slot.
hints: Is `PcoSemaphore` a strong or weak semaphore?
How many slots are needed for one waiting thread to proceed?

sections.title: 3. Case Study: PrinterManager (All 3 Stages & Deadlock Trap)
sections.description: From a race-prone first attempt, to the correct two-semaphore design, to the fatal lock-ordering deadlock.

blocks.title: Evolution of PrinterManager (Slides 30–34)
blocks.content:
`PrinterManager(int nbPrinters)` manages $N$ printers (`std::vector<bool> busy`) using `nbPrintersSem(nbPrinters)` to count available printers and `mutex(1)` for mutual exclusion. The slides walk through **3 stages**:

### Stage 1: Broken Attempt Without `mutex` (Slides 31–32)
* `allocate()` calls `nbPrintersSem.acquire(); return giveIndex();` and `giveBack()` sets `busy[index] = false; nbPrintersSem.release();`.
* **Bug:** Up to $N$ threads can enter `giveIndex()` **simultaneously**! Two threads can both scan `busy`, see `busy[0] == false`, and allocate the **exact same printer** (data race on `busy`).

### Stage 2: Correct Solution (Slide 33)
* Add `PcoSemaphore mutex(1);` to protect `giveIndex()` and the `busy[index] = false;` update in `giveBack()`.
* **Order in `allocate()`:** `nbPrintersSem.acquire()` **FIRST**, then `giveIndex()` (which acquires/releases `mutex`).
* **Order in `giveBack()`:** `mutex.acquire()` → `busy[index] = false;` → `mutex.release()` → `nbPrintersSem.release()`.
* **Self-Deadlock Note (Slide 33):** Even in this correct design, if a **single thread** allocates all $N$ printers and tries to allocate an $(N+1)$-th printer before calling `giveBack()`, it deadlocks on itself!

### Stage 3: Faulty Lock Ordering (Slide 34 — Deadlock!)
* If `allocate()` calls `mutex.acquire()` **before** `nbPrintersSem.acquire()`, and all $N$ printers are busy, the thread blocks on `nbPrintersSem.acquire()` **while still holding `mutex`**!
* When another thread calls `giveBack()` to return a printer, `giveBack()` calls `mutex.acquire()` before `nbPrintersSem.release()` → it blocks waiting for `mutex` → **permanent deadlock**!

blocks.title: PrinterManager: Correct Stage 2 vs. Faulty Stage 3 (Slides 33–34)

annotations.note: Wait for a free printer slot BEFORE acquiring mutex.
Slide 34 bug: acquiring mutex before nbPrintersSem.acquire() causes deadlock with giveBack().
giveBack() must acquire mutex to clear busy[index] before calling nbPrintersSem.release().

blocks.question: In Stage 3 of `PrinterManager` (Slide 34), `allocate()` calls `mutex.acquire()` BEFORE `nbPrintersSem.acquire()`, and `giveBack()` calls `mutex.acquire()` BEFORE `nbPrintersSem.release()`. When all printers are currently allocated, what happens if a thread calls `allocate()`?
options: Permanent deadlock: `allocate()` blocks on `nbPrintersSem.acquire()` while holding `mutex`, preventing any thread in `giveBack()` from acquiring `mutex` to release a printer.
It works fine as long as `PcoSemaphore` is a strong FIFO semaphore.
Two threads can allocate the same printer index, corrupting `busy`.
`giveBack()` skips `mutex` and releases `nbPrintersSem` immediately.
blocks.correct_answer: Permanent deadlock: `allocate()` blocks on `nbPrintersSem.acquire()` while holding `mutex`, preventing any thread in `giveBack()` from acquiring `mutex` to release a printer.
blocks.explanation: Never block on a resource-counting semaphore while holding a mutual-exclusion lock needed by the thread that releases the resource. `allocate()` holds `mutex` while waiting for `nbPrintersSem.release()`, and `giveBack()` cannot reach `nbPrintersSem.release()` because it is blocked on `mutex.acquire()`.
hints: Which semaphore does `allocate()` hold when it blocks on `nbPrintersSem.acquire()`?
What does `giveBack()` need to acquire before it can call `nbPrintersSem.release()`?

blocks.title: The Rendezvous Synchronization Pattern (Slide 39)
blocks.caption: Both TâcheA and TâcheB must complete their first activity (a1, b1) before EITHER can start its second activity (a2, b2).
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant TA as Tâche A
  participant TB as Tâche B
  Note over TA: Execute a1()
  Note over TB: Execute b1()
  TA->>TB: arriveA.release()
  TB->>TA: arriveB.release()
  Note over TA,TB: Rendezvous Point (Both synchronized!)
  Note over TA: Execute a2()
  Note over TB: Execute b2()

blocks.title: Rendezvous: Solution 1 (Slide 40), Solution 2 (Slide 41) & Broken Variant

annotations.note: In Slide 41, A calls acquire() first, but B calls release() first—so no deadlock!
B releases arriveB before calling acquire(arriveA), unblocking A.
If BOTH tasks call acquire() before release(), neither can ever reach release() -> deadlock.

blocks.title: Rendezvous Analysis: Why Slide 41 (Solution 2) Works vs. Symmetric Acquire-First
blocks.content:
With `static PcoSemaphore arriveA(0);` and `static PcoSemaphore arriveB(0);`:

| Variant | `myTaskA` | `myTaskB` | Outcome & Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Solution 1 (Slide 40)** | `a1(); arriveA.release(); arriveB.acquire(); a2();` | `b1(); arriveB.release(); arriveA.acquire(); b2();` | **Valid Rendezvous:** Both signal arrival *before* waiting. |
| **Solution 2 (Slide 41)** | `a1(); arriveB.acquire(); arriveA.release(); a2();` | `b1(); arriveB.release(); arriveA.acquire(); b2();` | **Valid Rendezvous (NO deadlock!):** `myTaskB` calls `arriveB.release()` **first**, unblocking `myTaskA` so it can call `arriveA.release()` and unblock `myTaskB`. Both `a1` and `b1` still finish before `a2` or `b2`! |
| **Broken Symmetric Acquire-First** | `a1(); arriveB.acquire(); arriveA.release(); a2();` | `b1(); arriveA.acquire(); arriveB.release(); b2();` | **Guaranteed Deadlock (*interblocage*):** Both call `acquire()` on `0`-initialized semaphores before either calls `release()`. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Careful Reading on Exams:** Always check whether **both** tasks call `acquire()` first, or only **one** does! In Slide 41's asymmetric Solution 2, `myTaskB` releases `arriveB` before acquiring `arriveA`, which breaks the circular wait.

blocks.title: Rendezvous: Asymmetric (Slide 41) vs. Symmetric Acquire-First
blocks.front: In Slide 41's Solution 2 (`myTaskA`: `arriveB.acquire(); arriveA.release();` and `myTaskB`: `arriveB.release(); arriveA.acquire();`), does it deadlock? Why or why not?
blocks.back:
**No, it does NOT deadlock—it is a valid asymmetric rendezvous!**

`myTaskB` calls `arriveB.release()` **first**, so `myTaskA` can pass `arriveB.acquire()` and then call `arriveA.release()`, which unblocks `myTaskB`. Both `a1()` and `b1()` are guaranteed to finish before either `a2()` or `b2()` starts.

Deadlock only occurs if **both** tasks call `acquire()` before `release()` (the symmetric `acquire`-first bug).
blocks.hint: Trace which semaphore `myTaskB` operates on first.

blocks.question: In Slide 41 (Solution 2), `arriveA(0)` and `arriveB(0)` start at `0`. `myTaskA` runs `a1(); arriveB.acquire(); arriveA.release(); a2();` and `myTaskB` runs `b1(); arriveB.release(); arriveA.acquire(); b2();`. What happens?
options: Valid rendezvous (no deadlock): both `a1()` and `b1()` always complete before either `a2()` or `b2()` starts.
Guaranteed deadlock (interblocage): both threads block forever on `acquire()`.
`a2()` can execute before `b1()` finishes.
`b2()` can execute before `a1()` finishes.
blocks.correct_answer: Valid rendezvous (no deadlock): both `a1()` and `b1()` always complete before either `a2()` or `b2()` starts.
blocks.explanation: Because `myTaskB` calls `arriveB.release()` BEFORE `arriveA.acquire()`, it unblocks `myTaskA` at `arriveB.acquire()`. `myTaskA` then calls `arriveA.release()`, unblocking `myTaskB`. Neither `a2()` nor `b2()` can start until both `a1()` and `b1()` have completed.
hints: Look closely at `myTaskB`: does it call `acquire()` or `release()` first?
Can `a2()` start before `myTaskB` calls `arriveB.release()`? Can `b2()` start before `myTaskA` calls `arriveA.release()`?

sections.title: 5. End-of-Chapter Exercises (Slides 43–44)
sections.description: Implementing a mutex with semaphores, local vs. static PcoMutex, and main-thread start signaling.

blocks.title: Exercise 1 (Slide 43): Implementing a Mutex Using Only Semaphores

annotations.note: A bare PcoSemaphore(1) alone is NOT a mutex because it lacks ownership and counts extra releases!
Only the thread that acquired the lock may release it; extra unlocks are ignored.

blocks.title: Exercise 1 Self-Check: Why `PcoSemaphore(1)` Alone Is Not a Mutex
blocks.prompt: Why is a single `PcoSemaphore sem(1)` insufficient to implement a true mutex (Slide 43, Exercise 1), and what extra state is required to preserve mutex semantics?
self_check_criteria: Noted that a bare `PcoSemaphore(1)` has no concept of an owner thread, so another thread could call `release()`.

Noted that calling `release()` multiple times on a `PcoSemaphore(1)` increments its counter above 1 (allowing multiple threads into the critical section), whereas extra `unlock()` calls on a mutex have no effect.
Included tracking the `owner` thread ID and `locked` boolean (protected by an internal binary semaphore) so `unlock()` only releases `sem` when `locked && owner == currentThread`.
blocks.model_answer: A bare `PcoSemaphore(1)` does not track ownership and counts every `release()` (so two `release()` calls would raise the counter to 2 and break mutual exclusion). To preserve mutex semantics, we store a `locked` flag and `owner` thread ID protected by a small internal `stateLock(1)` semaphore, and only call `sem.release()` in `unlock()` if `locked` is true and the caller is `owner`.

blocks.title: Exercise 2 (Slide 43): Local PcoMutex vs. static PcoMutex

annotations.note: Each thread gets its own unlocked PcoMutex on its stack -> zero mutual exclusion!
static allocates one shared PcoMutex in static storage, synchronizing all threads calling tache_correct().

blocks.title: Exercise 3 (Slide 44): Main-Thread Start Signal for 2 Tasks

annotations.note: Alternatively, a single `PcoSemaphore start(0)` can be used if `main()` calls `start.release()` TWICE (once per waiting task).

blocks.title: Exercises 2 & 3 Self-Check: Shared Scope & Counting Signals
blocks.prompt: 1) Why does `PcoMutex mutex;` inside `void tache()` fail while `static PcoMutex mutex;` works? 2) In Exercise 3, if you used a single `PcoSemaphore start(0)` instead of two semaphores, what happens if `main()` only calls `start.release()` once?
self_check_criteria: Explained that a local `PcoMutex` lives on each thread's private stack (separate objects), whereas `static PcoMutex` creates one shared object in static memory.
Explained that `release()` wakes only ONE waiting thread, so a single `start.release()` would leave the second task blocked forever—`main()` must call `release()` twice (or use two semaphores).
blocks.model_answer: 1) A local variable is allocated on each thread's own stack, so every thread locks its own private mutex and enters the critical section simultaneously. `static` creates a single shared mutex instance. 2) Each `release()` increments the semaphore by 1 and wakes at most one blocked thread; with two tasks waiting on `start.acquire()`, calling `release()` only once leaves one task permanently blocked.

blocks.question: Two threads concurrently call `void tache() { PcoMutex mutex; mutex.lock(); std::cout << "Section critique" << std::endl; mutex.unlock(); }`. What happens?
options: Both threads can enter the `std::cout` line simultaneously because each thread creates its own local `PcoMutex` on its stack.
Mutual exclusion is guaranteed because `PcoMutex` automatically shares state by variable name.
The second thread deadlocks on `mutex.lock()`.
A compiler error occurs because `PcoMutex` cannot be declared inside a function.
blocks.correct_answer: Both threads can enter the `std::cout` line simultaneously because each thread creates its own local `PcoMutex` on its stack.
blocks.explanation: Local variables inside a function are allocated per-call on each thread's private stack. To synchronize threads, the `PcoMutex` must be shared (`static`, global, or a shared object member).
hints: Where do local variables live in memory for each thread?
Do the two threads lock the same `PcoMutex` instance or two different ones?
